planting.note: Plant rooted divisions directly into saturated soil or up to a few inches of standing water along pond and stream margins in spring. Established stands spread readily by rhizome, so site it where a colonizing groundcover is wanted.

directions: Common spikerush forms leafless, rounded green stems topped by small brown spikelets, resembling a fine-textured rush more than a typical sedge. It naturally colonizes shallow pond edges, ditches, and wet meadows across most of North America and is valued in constructed wetlands and rain gardens for erosion control and waterfowl habitat. It spreads aggressively by rhizome in consistently wet or flooded soil, so give it room or contain it in a water garden. Cut back matted growth in late winter to refresh the stand before spring regrowth.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Press small plugs or rooted runners into wet mud or shallow water at a pond margin; it spreads quickly by fine rhizomes to form a dense turf-like mat.

directions: Needle spikerush is a diminutive, hair-fine relative of the bulrushes that forms a low, grass-like carpet in shallow water or saturated soil. It is widely used in aquariums and small water gardens as a living lawn substitute because it stays short and tolerates being fully submerged. In outdoor pond margins it knits together loose sediment and provides cover for small aquatic invertebrates. It spreads by slender rhizomes and can be divided and replanted whenever a denser patch is wanted elsewhere.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to saturated soil in spring; established clumps spread steadily by rhizome to form colonies.

directions: Baltic rush is a circumboreal native with slender, blue-green, unbranched stems that rise from creeping rhizomes to form loose colonies rather than tight clumps. It tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than many rushes, growing in everything from wet meadows to seasonally dry alkaline flats, which makes it a dependable choice for rain gardens and prairie pothole restoration. Small brown flower clusters appear partway up the stem in early summer. Because it spreads by rhizome, give it room to naturalize or plant it where a colonizing groundcover is desired.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plugs into consistently moist to boggy soil or shallow water at a pond edge in spring; clumps thicken over a season or two without becoming as spreading as Baltic rush.

directions: Dagger-leaf rush is distinctive among rushes for its flattened, iris-like leaf blades rather than the round hollow stems typical of Juncus effusus. In mid to late summer it produces dark brown to nearly black rounded flower clusters held above the foliage, giving it strong textural and color contrast in pond-edge and bog plantings. It forms a tidy, clump-forming habit that is better behaved in small water features than more aggressively spreading rushes. Native to wet meadows and streambanks of western North America, it appreciates consistent moisture and light shade in hotter climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions in saturated soil or up to a foot of standing water at a pond or wetland margin; give it plenty of room since it forms large rhizomatous colonies.

directions: Hardstem bulrush, known in the western United States as tule, is a tall, round-stemmed native emergent that forms dense stands in shallow lakes, marshes, and pond margins. Its stiff, cylindrical green stems provide critical nesting and cover habitat for waterfowl and marsh birds, and historically the stems were used by Indigenous peoples for weaving mats, baskets, and boats. It spreads by thick rhizomes to form extensive colonies, making it best suited to large water gardens or wetland restoration rather than small ponds. Small brown spikelet clusters appear near the stem tips in summer.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring after the danger of hard frost has passed; site it where its vigorous spreading habit can be contained, such as with a root barrier.

directions: Amur silvergrass is a large, coarse-textured relative of maiden grass that spreads by vigorous rhizomes rather than forming a tight clump, and it is considerably more cold-hardy and earlier-flowering than most Miscanthus sinensis cultivars. Silvery-white plumes emerge above the foliage in late summer, well before typical maiden grass cultivars bloom, aging to a fluffy tan by fall. Because of its running habit it is best used for large-scale screening, erosion control on slopes, or biomass plantings rather than in tight garden borders, and it has naturalized in parts of the eastern United States. Cut the dried foliage back hard in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant container transplants after frost danger has passed; it is grown as an annual outside zones 8-10.

directions: Feathertop grass produces soft, fluffy, creamy-white to pale green bottlebrush plumes on gently arching stems from midsummer through fall, and it is one of the most popular ornamental grasses for cutting and drying. Native to arid grasslands of northeastern Africa, it is a tender perennial grown as a warm-season annual across most of the country, thriving in heat and lean, well-drained soil. It self-sows readily where winters are mild, sometimes to the point of becoming a minor garden weed, so deadhead spent plumes if volunteer seedlings are unwanted. In frost-free zones it persists as a short-lived clumping perennial.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall for natural stratification, or set out container plants in spring; establish in lean, well-drained soil and avoid summer irrigation once roots are established.

directions: Idaho fescue forms neat, fine-textured tufts of blue-green to gray-green foliage that stay evergreen through mild winters, with slender flowering stalks rising above the clump in early summer. It is a keystone bunchgrass of Pacific Northwest and Intermountain West prairies and open pine forests, prized in native plant gardens and restoration seedings for its drought tolerance and role as a larval host for several native butterflies. Once established it needs little supplemental water and resents heavy summer irrigation or soggy winter soil. Light grooming to remove old foliage in early spring keeps clumps looking tidy.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall or plant container-grown starts in fall or early spring in part shade with well-drained soil; established clumps tolerate summer dry shade once rooted in.

directions: California fescue is a larger, more shade-tolerant relative of the familiar blue fescues, forming graceful arching mounds of blue-gray to soft green foliage under oaks and in dry woodland settings. Delicate, airy flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring, aging to a warm tan by summer. It is one of the best clumping grasses for dry shade in California gardens, tolerating little to no summer water once established beneath established trees. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth begins to keep the clump looking fresh.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil; divide every few years to keep clumps vigorous and prevent dead centers.

directions: Large blue fescue forms denser, larger tussocks of fine blue-green to steel-blue foliage than the more common Festuca glauca, and is noted for its violet-tinged flower spikelets that rise on wiry stems in early summer before fading to tan. It performs well in rock gardens, edging, and mass plantings where its tidy mounded form and cool color read well against darker foliage. It is intolerant of wet, heavy soil, especially in winter, and benefits from gritty, well-drained sites. Shear off old flower stalks after they fade and comb out dead blades in spring to maintain a neat mound.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
